task: For this synthetic writing exercise, use the fictional reporting notes to write a reported feature for a general newspaper audience. Write from this reporting snapshot as of April 8, 2025. Include a headline. Target 450 to 650 words. Follow AP style.

facts.text: Lowland County, a fictional coastal county in North Carolina, began buying out flood-prone homes in 2019 and converting the acquired land to wetlands. Its April 2025 review describes the completed purchases, remaining owners and program finances.
Hurricane Marion, a Category 3 storm, struck the county in September 2017, flooding approximately 800 homes, many for the second or third time.
The county launched its buyout program in early 2019 using $62 million from a FEMA Hazard Mitigation Grant and an $18 million county match, for a total program budget of $80 million.
The program offered homeowners 105 percent of their property's pre-flood assessed value, with the extra 5 percent intended to help cover relocation costs.
By April 2025, the county had completed 240 buyouts; the properties have been demolished and converted to approximately 340 acres of restored coastal wetland.
County Emergency Manager Robert Yates said: "Six years later, the neighborhoods that moved do not flood. The ones that stayed do."

Of the roughly 800 homes originally targeted, 112 property owners declined to sell; those properties flooded in both 2019 and 2022. Beyond the 240 completed buyouts and 112 refusals, the notes do not classify the other initially targeted properties.
Homeowners who declined buyouts faced an average of approximately $34,000 in flood repair costs per storm event.
Delia Marsh, 71, who inherited her home from her parents and has lived there her entire life, declined the buyout. She said: "This is where I was born and this is where I intend to stay."
The buyout program took six years instead of the projected three, partly because of title disputes on 47 properties that required legal resolution.

County engineers modeled lower peak flood levels behind the restored wetland than in a comparison without restoration. The packet provides no universal storm-surge reduction figure or guarantee of protection in every storm.

Among the structures on bought-out land was the former Shoreline Community Elementary School, closed since 2016 due to flood damage, and the Shoreline Diner, a local gathering place that had operated for 38 years.

Neighboring Coastal Pines County rejected managed retreat after Hurricane Marion and instead spent $45 million on levee repairs and beach nourishment; it experienced significant flooding again in 2022.

Dr. Maya Santos, a researcher at fictional North Coastal University who has studied the program for four years, said the long-term effectiveness of managed retreat depends heavily on where displaced residents relocate and whether they find comparable housing affordability.
Santos's research found that of the 240 households that sold, roughly 60 percent remained within the county; 40 percent relocated to other regions, some leaving North Carolina entirely.

Congress is debating whether to require localities to adopt managed retreat plans as a condition for renewing participation in the National Flood Insurance Program; Lowland County officials have testified in favor.

Yates estimated that repeated disaster recovery, infrastructure repair and flood insurance supplementation for the 240 bought-out properties would have cost approximately $112 million over six years. He compared that counterfactual estimate with the program's $80 million authorized budget, not a supplied final expenditure total.
The county has no plans to expand the buyout program; the remaining $3.1 million in unspent FEMA funds reverted to the federal government in January 2025.
Two of the 112 holdout homeowners have since approached the county asking to sell; the county has no current program to accommodate them.
Marsh said she had flood insurance and had repaired her home twice since 2017 but declined to say how much she had spent or received in insurance payments.
Lowland County has a population of approximately 18,000; Hurricane Marion caused an estimated $340 million in total property damage in the county.
The county's experience has been cited by FEMA and the fictional Coastal Resilience Coalition as a model for communities facing repeated flood cycles.

A county consultant's 2024 model estimated that the restored wetland would retain approximately 280,000 gallons of runoff in one specified rain event. This is a modeled volume for that scenario, not a measurement of storm-surge height or a guarantee for every storm.
